title: Sports & Entertainment: 53k to 745k Addressable Audience
excerpt: A national sports precinct grew its addressable audience fourteenfold using cookieless personas, with campaigns 20-30% better on CPA. Read the case.
rm_desc: Cookieless audience building grew reach fourteenfold and cut CPA 20-30% for a sports venue. Read the case.
content: This cookieless audience building case covers a national sports and entertainment precinct whose addressable audience stood at 53,000 defined individuals, far short of what its venue calendar needed to fill.

Cookieless personas were constructed from first-party and contextual signals, with segmentation mapped to event categories rather than demographics alone. Campaigns then ran continuously against the defined segments, with CPA and ROAS tracked per segment and reported with their limitations named.
Why cookieless audience building, not third-party data

Third-party cookie deprecation was already reshaping how the ad industry targets audiences when this engagement started, and a precinct depending on rented, third-party segments would have seen its addressable reach shrink over time rather than grow. Building first-party, contextual audiences instead meant the asset belonged to the client rather than to a data broker whose supply could disappear with a policy change. That durability is the actual point of cookieless audience building, beyond being a workaround for a deprecated targeting method.
The addressable audience grew from 53k to 745k defined individuals. Ongoing campaigns against those segments run 20–30% better on CPA, with platform-reported ROAS above 400%.

Platform-reported is said deliberately: ROAS a platform grades for itself flatters, and incrementality is the harder, better question, we will tell you when a number is which. The durable asset here is the audience itself, not any single campaign built on top of it. The media results follow from the cookieless audience building work, and the engagement is ongoing, so the figures describe a running programme rather than a closed one.
What this does not prove for every venue

A fourteenfold audience increase depended on a specific starting condition: a precinct with a wide event calendar and enough first-party touchpoints, ticketing, membership, on-site Wi-Fi, to build contextual segments from. A smaller venue with fewer events and less first-party data would build a smaller addressable audience through the same cookieless audience building method, and the multiple would be lower. The method transfers; the specific multiple does not.

Cookieless audience building sits inside our broader analytics and data work; the ongoing campaigns built on top of it run through paid media. Venues and event operators considering a similar cookieless audience building programme can start with either service page to see the full scope.

Ticketing history, membership records, on-site Wi-Fi authentication and contextual signals from the content people engaged with on owned channels, all first-party, all consented at the point of collection. None of it depended on a third-party cookie or a data broker's panel, which is precisely why the resulting cookieless audience building programme kept working through the platform-level targeting changes that disrupted campaigns built on rented data elsewhere in the industry.

The jump from 53,000 to 745,000 defined individuals was not a single migration event, it accumulated across several event cycles as more first-party touchpoints fed the segmentation model and the model itself improved at distinguishing event-category interest from generic attendance. Cookieless audience building of this kind rewards patience over a quick platform swap; the venues that try to shortcut the accumulation period typically end up with a smaller, less reliable and less durable audience than the one that was built properly and patiently from the start.
Client described rather than named, and all figures are reported exactly as recorded at the time.
